rationale: A wins because it has discipline: "On will rent you a running shoe you can never own" is a sharp retail/business story, and the set keeps accountability, materials, and runner lenses in separate rooms. B has usable pieces, but "Shoes join the rental economy: On's nationwide subscription as a bet on product-as-a-service" is the same ownership angle in a jargon coat, then it pads into "does the rest of the running category have to follow?" without competitor evidence. A also polices its own weak spots, especially the line that the recycling-rate angle is "a question, not a story" without return data; B notices the gaps but still pitches around them too freely.
gaps_in_A: "this model hands the retirement decision to the brand" goes past the facts. The return trigger is unknown, and A later admits it needs that proof.
"is a demand signal for an agricultural supply chain" is a touch too grand without unit volume, sourcing, or production forecast. The angle is viable, but the claim needs a shorter leash.

"the ownership/category angle is the strongest and needs the least missing proof" undersells how much is still missing: monthly price, contract terms, non-return rules, and pilot conversion all matter.
gaps_in_B: "On bets runners will pay monthly to never own their shoes" and "Shoes join the rental economy" are the same ownership/subscription story split into two envelopes. That is padding, not distinctness.
"moving a core product line to this model" is not grounded. The update says Cyclon is getting a nationwide subscription, not that On is moving a core product line.
"does a nationwide rollout prove shoppers will accept access-not-ownership" is a trap. The update gives no subscriber count, conversion rate, retention, or demand data.

"does the rest of the running category have to follow?" manufactures competitive pressure from one fact: On is fast-growing. No named competitors, no analyst signal, no evidence the category is reacting.
